name: A Tale of Two Middle Classes
description:
How has the transformation of the Indian economy over the 21st century shaped the lives of ordinary Indians?  
This talk traces the evolution of India’s middle classes through data from the India Human Development Survey, a study that repeatedly interviewed more than 40,000 households between 2004 and 2024. Grounded in these lived experiences, the talk examines the size and origins of both the upper and lower middle classes, exploring their lifestyles and aspirations as they navigate a changing, and at times uncertain, economy. 
This lecture is a part of Azim Premji University’s Public Lecture Series.

name: Crystal & Ash
description:
Are relics more than static remnants of the past? 
This lecture on the relics of the Buddha excavated from the ancient stupa at Piprahwa, traces their long, contested journey to reveal the deep entanglement of material culture, belief, and power across history and into the present. 
Excavated in 1898 and removed from India for over a century, the Piprahwa relics have been shrouded in controversy, from disputes over authenticity to competing claims of ownership and attempted auctions. Their recent return brings new urgency to old questions. Naman P. Ahuja will explain how relics are defined in Buddhist tradition, their role in geopolitics through what scholars call “relic diplomacy,” the legal shifts shaping their custody, and what all this means for museums today.

name: How the Partition Reshaped Indian Politics
description:
The early republic chose liberty over equality, and Heartland Rising argues that it was the wrong choice.  
In this session Javed Gaya presents his book, a searing examination of the forces driving India’s contemporary majoritarian turn, followed by a discussion with Aakar Patel on liberty and equality. 
From the upheavals of the 1940s, including Partition and the framing of the Constitution, to the present, Gaya revisits a foundational debate: should India be anchored in liberty, defined as “one man, one vote,” or equality, understood as meaningful political representation for minorities in a federal structure? He argues that the early republic’s choice of liberty over equality is why contemporary India now finds itself with neither. Gaya maps how Partition and the elevation of the Hindi heartland reshaped India’s social and economic trajectory, amplifying caste and communal divisions, weakening the judiciary and federalism, and narrowing the space for pluralism. 
Venue: Library

name: Din Din Anand
description:
What do midday and mid-octave have in common? 
This Hindustani classical concert traces the ancient bond between melody, time of day, and the rhythms of nature. The science has been carried by the Shastras through generations, where ragas rise and fall with the turning of the day. 
The Shastras divide the day into eight three-hour blocks, or prahars, mirroring the eight notes of an octave. Each prahar calls for ragas suited to invoke a particular state of mind; experienced consecutively, the impact is undeniable. Renowned vocalist Nishad Baakre leads the performance, accompanied by Bheemashankar Bidanur on Tabla and Tejas Ravindra Katoti on Harmonium.

name: The Siachen Glacier - Managing Mountains and War
description:
Inside the world’s highest, harshest battlefield, this talk covers not only the mountains but the war, politics, financial cost, and human toll of the ongoing conflict in Siachen. Here, India, Pakistan, and China have been engaged in hostilities for decades. The talk includes over 180 photographs documenting the Siachen Glacier and the people involved. 
Drawing on visits to the region since 1980, including reaching Karakoram Pass, Col Italia, and Indira Col, the three northernmost points of India, the talk traces the Indian Army’s role in the glacier, the young soldiers who serve there, and the sacrifices they make. It considers the challenges civilian expeditions face on the glacier, questions of leadership, and a proposal for a “Siachen Peace Park” to end the conflict. Though a ceasefire holds today, soldiers continue to endure the glacier’s harsh conditions. 
In collaboration with: 
The Himalayan Club
Founded in 1928, the Himalayan Club is one of the earliest mountaineering clubs established in the subcontinent, with a presence across India and abroad. Its objectives extend beyond climbing to publications, awards, lectures, social activities, sponsorships, and mountain film festivals. First published in 1928, The Himalayan Journal has earned worldwide recognition as the most reliable reference on the Himalaya, Karakoram, and Hindukush. Members include some of the most decorated mountaineers and explorers in India and abroad. The club will soon celebrate its centenary year! 
 
Venue: Seminar Halls

name: Thinking Ecologically about Our Common Future
description:
Can we protect, restore, and create ecosystems faster than we are building over them? 
Harini Nagendra, ecologist and author, returns to BIC nearly two decades after her 2010 talk here, to ask the same question in a city transformed. 
In 2010, Nagendra warned that climate change and urbanization together would overwhelm old, top-down models of conservation. Today,  protected-area-focused thinking is inadequate for the crisis facing Indian cities. In Bangalore specifically, the starkest change has been the devastation of peri-urban ecology, alongside deepening social inequality and a widening disconnect between people and nature in the city. 
This talk is part of a series marking twenty years of BIC, in which speakers and artists from the institution’s early years return to revisit the topics they first addressed. Each session traces what has changed, what has endured, and what to make of the same topics two decades on.

name: The Trembling Tiber
description:
A contemporary voice echoes with Shakespeare’s language; a dialogue across four centuries. 
Neal Hall reads from The Trembling Tiber, his award-winning poetry collection that enters into a conversation with Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar. The reading is followed by a discussion with Arul Mani, and an audience Q&A. 
The collection emerged during Hall’s residency as an Artist-in-Residence at the American Academy in Rome, after he was stopped at gunpoint by Italian Special Forces while walking through an all-white area of the city on the Ides of March. That convergence of place, history, and date became the catalyst for this work, which is not an adaptation of Julius Caesar but a conversation with it, in which the past speaks to the present and the present answers back.

name: Decoding Behavioural Insights
description:
Incentives and institutions, culture and power — this panel discussion examines the intersection of behavioural science, public purpose, and corporate decision-making in contemporary India, centred around Sutapa Banerjee’s new book The Business of Business is (Not) Just Business. 
Behavioural economics, the study of judgement and decision-making, has a rich academic history and practical applications across nearly every part of human experience. As public policy think tanks and corporate consultancies increasingly adopt and adapt this research, understanding its core principles has become more important than ever. Drawing on examples from the Indian context, the panel illustrates the relevance and multidisciplinary reach of behavioural insights in shaping both institutions and everyday decisions.

name: Through the Adivasi Gaze
description:
Aabua Paika Kabu Bageya: We Won’t Let Go of Our Paika! | 26 mins |  Mundari | 2017 | India 
This film screening and panel discussion explores the critical role of self-representation in reclaiming cultural identity. What changes when Adivasi culture is conveyed by Adivasis themselves, rather than through an outside lens? 
The program opens with a screening of the documentary Aabua Paika Kabu Bageya: We Won’t Let Go of Our Paika!, centring on Paika, a traditional Munda martial art dance form that serves as a living archive of historical struggle, triumph, and resilience. A panel discussion follows, marking a fundamental shift in perspective: moving away from the historic, colonial lens to honour the Adivasi gaze. Tribal culture, the panel argues, is not a static object to be documented by outsiders or kept in museums, but a dynamic, living identity best understood through narratives produced directly by members of the community themselves. The event concludes with an audience Q&A.

name: Yayati - Life and Desire
description:
How far will a man go to prolong a life of indulgence? 
This Kuttiyattam performance interweaves the special pakarnnattam technique with dance to tell the story of Yayati. 
Drawing on the Mahabharata, the Puranas, V. S. Khandekar’s celebrated novel, and Girish Karnad’s play, the story unfolds as Yayati openly marries Devayani, daughter of Shukracharya, preceptor of the Asuras, and her friend, the Asura princess Sharmishtha, in secret. Bound by worldly pleasure, he goes so far as to borrow his own son’s youth to prolong his indulgence. Will he reckon with the cost of his greed?

name: Working Girls
description:
133 min | Tamil, Hindi, Bangla, Marathi, Malayalam and Telugu with English subtitles | 2005 
Invisible women, seen through the lens of wit, humour and dignity. 
Domestic workers, farmers, mothers, ASHA workers, dancers, and organisers all labour to sustain society but are rarely acknowledged. Working Girls is a vivid, genre-defying documentary that traverses India to uncover the invisible yet essential work performed by women. From care work and domestic work to surrogacy and sex work, the film challenges dominant ideas about labour, value, and visibility. 
It was filmed across the country in Kolkata, Mumbai, Shillong, Latur, Thiruvananthapuram, Hyderabad and Madurai. The film is directed by Paromita Vohra and created in collaboration with the Laws of Social Reproduction project. The Laws of Social Reproduction project, led by Prabha Kotiswaran at King’s College London, draws on feminist legal theory to study women’s reproductive labour, and how law renders this labour invisible, proposing reform toward economic justice for women.

description:
Inspired by real conversations with her granddaughter, and her debut picture book We Are Family, Sujatha Balakrishnan creates a warm and welcoming space for children to celebrate different kinds of families. Through storytelling, conversation and playful activities, the session aims to normalise conversations around adoption with openness, curiosity and empathy, helping children discover that love is what truly makes a family. 
Around the World in 50 Sundays is a journey that begins, not with a ticket, but with opening a book. In a city like Bangalore where families are always in motion, the BIC Library hopes to offer stillness and a quiet, welcoming space for both parents and children where reading becomes a shared experience. Every Sunday, we open our doors to invite you into a library that listens; building a rhythm of return, a habit of joy and a new community bound not just by books, but by the weekly ritual of reading together.

name: Losing Words, Losing Worlds
description:
If you can predict it, you can name it. 
Across India, hundreds of words in local dialects capture the specific rhythms of regional climate: a short drizzle versus a multi-day downpour, particular cloud formations, the first signs of a temperature spike. This talk looks at what it means when those words start to disappear, and what that loss says about our relationship to the natural world. 
India’s climate discourse is largely conducted in English, top-down, and removed from the lived reality of those most affected by the crisis. As weather patterns grow more erratic, the environmental phenomena they once reliably described are disappearing too, and with them, the language and knowledge. A pilot study across twenty-two languages and fifteen states found that farmers, fisherfolk, and forest-dependent communities report over a hundred vernacular terms fading from use, taking entire systems of ecological literacy with them. Language, this project argues, is infrastructure essential to grassroots resilience and locally grounded climate solutions. 
Venue: Seminar Halls
